title: Brownian Motion
intro: Brownian motion is a random walk taken to the limit of infinitely many tiny steps. Its paths are continuous but nowhere differentiable, its increments are independent normals, and it is the foundation of stochastic calculus.

blocks.text: A standard Brownian motion (Wiener process) $B(t)$, $t\ge0$, satisfies:

items: Independent increments: $B(t) - B(s)$ is independent of the path up to time $s$.
Normal increments: $B(t) - B(s)\sim N(0, t - s)$.

blocks.text: It follows that $\operatorname{Cov}(B(s), B(t)) = \min(s, t)$. Donsker's theorem makes the random-walk picture precise: a simple random walk with $n$ steps, rescaled by $1/\sqrt n$ in space and $1/n$ in time, converges to Brownian motion. Wiener constructed it rigorously in 1923; physically it is Einstein's 1905 model of a pollen grain buffeted by molecules.

items: Nowhere differentiable: the increment over time $h$ is of size $\sqrt h$, so difference quotients blow up like $1/\sqrt h$.
Quadratic variation: summing squared increments over a fine partition of $[0, t]$ gives exactly $t$, not 0 as for a smooth path. Formally $(dB)^2 = dt$, the rule behind Itô's formula.
Scaling: $c^{-1/2}B(ct)$ is again a standard Brownian motion, so the paths look statistically the same at every zoom level.
Reflection principle: $P\left(\max_{s\le t}B(s)\ge a\right) = 2P(B(t)\ge a)$, since every path that reaches $a$ can be reflected after its first hitting time.

blocks.text: Adding drift and scale gives $X(t) = \mu t + \sigma B(t)$; exponentiating gives geometric Brownian motion, the Black–Scholes model of stock prices. Stochastic differential equations $dX = a(X)\,dt + b(X)\,dB$ model diffusions in physics, biology and finance; their densities satisfy the Fokker–Planck equation, and the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process (a mean-reverting Brownian motion) is the continuous-time cousin of an autoregressive model and of a leaky integrator.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(29)
n, paths = 1000, 20000
dB = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(1 / n), (paths, n))      # increments over [0, 1]
B = np.cumsum(dB, axis=1)
print(f"Var B(1) = {B[:, -1].var():.4f} (1), Var B(1/2) = {B[:, n//2 - 1].var():.4f} (1/2)")
print(f"Cov(B(1/4), B(3/4)) = {np.cov(B[:, n//4 - 1], B[:, 3*n//4 - 1])[0, 1]:.4f} (min(s,t) = 1/4)")
# Quadratic variation: the sum of squared increments over [0, 1] equals t = 1, path by path
print(f"sum of (dB)^2 on one path: {np.sum(dB[0] ** 2):.4f}; spread across paths {np.std((dB ** 2).sum(1)):.4f}")
# Reflection principle: P(max_{t<=1} B(t) > a) = 2 P(B(1) > a)
a = 1.0
print(f"P(max B > 1): simulated {np.mean(B.max(1) > a):.4f}, reflection 2 P(B(1) > 1) = {2 * stats.norm.sf(a):.4f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: from 20 000 discretised paths, $\operatorname{Var}B(1) = 0.995$, $\operatorname{Var}B(1/2) = 0.496$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(B(1/4), B(3/4)) = 0.248$, matching $t$ and $\min(s, t)$. The sum of squared increments on one path is 1.009, with a spread across paths of only 0.045: quadratic variation is essentially deterministic. The probability that the maximum exceeds 1 is 0.304 by simulation against 0.317 from the reflection principle; the discretised paths miss excursions between grid points, so they slightly undercount.

blocks.title: Scaling
blocks.text: Show that $W(t) = \tfrac12B(4t)$ is a standard Brownian motion (check the variance of its increments).
solution: $W(t) - W(s) = \tfrac12(B(4t) - B(4s))\sim N(0, \tfrac14\cdot4(t - s)) = N(0, t - s)$.
Independence of increments and continuity carry over, so $W$ is a standard Brownian motion.
